newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African wage increases below inflation in Q1.
newsitem.headline: S.African wage increases below inflation in Q1.

text.p: South African wage settlements during the first quarter of the year averaged 9.1 percent, below the average inflation rate of 9.6 percent for the year to date, according to a survey released on Monday.

Indications are that the remaining wage rounds will be marked by tough talking from both employers and unions, although analysts said wage increases were unlikely to be substantially higher than the first quarter for the rest of 1997.

An interim wage report by industrial relations consultants Andrew Levy & Associates showed settlements ranged from eight percent to 12.5 percent across industries with the average minimum wage at 1,675.00 rand.
Last year's first quarter average was 10 percent.
Andrew Levy research associate Jackie Kelly expects remaining talks to be difficult as both employers and unions attempt to stand their ground.

"Employers are digging in their heels, while on the part of unions, who are under pressure from their members, there is perhaps a realisation that the economic climate is such that higher settlements are not feasible at this stage," Kelly said.

She said while wage bargaining was still at an early stage, initial results reflected the perception that times were tough and final settlements would not be substantially higher than the first quarter average.
In one of the first wage deals struck this year, workers and employers at food and beverage group Nestle SA settled on a minimum increase of 9.0 percent after a four-week strike.
Labour analysts said the agreement, reached after both parties adopted a tough stance, could set the tone for settlement levels in the industry.

Average first quarter wage deals reached with major unions affiliated to the country's largest trade union federation, the Congress of South African Trade Unions, include 11 percent with the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM) and 9.5 percent with the National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa (Numsa).
In the public sector, the average settlement reached with the National Education Health and Allied Workers Union (NEHAWU) was 8.2 percent.
In a recent collective bargaining survey, industrial relations consultants Gavin Brown & Associates noted the most important talks this year would centre on the public sector.

Unions would be faced with uncertainties of accelerating privatisation initiatives, sub-inflationary wage increases and retrenchments linked to government's intention to reduce public sector employment at a central and regional level.
"All these factors combine to suggest that we may expect the highest levels of industrial action in 1997 to occur in public sector," the survey said.
